Administrative Process This policy applies to HealthPartners Self Insured Commercial plans, except for the level funded block of business. Coverage Spinal decompression surgeries are generally covered subject to the indications listed below and per your plan documents. Indications that are covered without prior authorization Cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spinal decompression surgeries are considered medically necessary for any of the following conditions: • Epidural compression or vertebral destruction from tumor • Idiopathic scoliosis • Instability after debridement for infection • Neural compression after spinal fracture • Pseudarthrosis • Spinal infections (including tuberculosis, osteomyelitis, discitis) • Acute cauda equina or acute spinal cord compression syndrome • Acute spinal fracture from documented trauma • Intra-operative spinal instability Coverage Criteria Cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spinal decompression surgeries are covered when all of the following criteria are met: 1. Clinical documentation indicates presence/diagnosis of a condition or conditions causing spinal cord and/or nerve root compression. The following list includes possible conditions and is not all-inclusive. A. Spinal stenosis B. Spondylolisthesis C. Spondylosis D. Spinal cyst E. Osteophytes F. Herniated disc, and 2. Clinical documentation indicates presence of at least one sign/symptom, associated with the condition(s), limiting activities of daily living. The following list includes possible signs/symptoms and is not all-inclusive. A. Radiculopathy B. Neurogenic claudication C. Myelopathy D. Upper/lower extremity weakness, numbness, or pain, and 3. Clinical documentation includes radiographic results (e.g., plain radiographs, advanced imaging studies), confirming the presence of spinal cord and/or nerve root compression caused by the condition(s) and supporting the indication for the decompression surgery, and 4. Clinical documentation shows the sign(s)/symptom(s), identified in criterion 2 above, persist despite completion of at least 8 weeks of intensive conservative treatments (such as exercise, medication use, or chiropractic care). Documentation of conservative treatments must correspond to the current episode of care (within 6 months). A. Active muscle conditioning is required as part of physical therapy. Physical therapist’s notes must be submitted. Note: The requirement for physical therapy will not be met if there is a failure to complete prescribed physical therapy for non-clinical reasons. There must be a physician’s statement in the clinical documents that explains why physical therapy is contraindicated. Repeat/Reoperation cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spinal decompression surgeries, at the same site/location as the index/initial decompression surgery, are covered when all of the following criteria are met: 1. Clinical documentation indicates presence of at least one sign/symptom, associated with the condition(s), limiting activities of daily living. The following list includes possible signs/symptoms and is not all-inclusive. A. Radiculopathy B. Neurogenic claudication C. Myelopathy D. Upper/lower extremity weakness, numbness, or pain, and 3. Radiographic documentation (plain radiographs, advanced imaging studies), confirming the presence of spinal cord and/or nerve root compression caused by the condition(s) and supporting the indication for the decompression surgery. Indications that are not covered 1. All laser spine decompression procedures, including, but not limited to, laser discectomy (also known as laser-assisted discectomy, laser disc decompression, or laser-assisted disc decompression [LADD]) (62287), percutaneous laser discectomy (62287), laparoscopic laser discectomy, endoscopic laser foraminoplasty, endoscopic laser foraminotomy, endoscopic laser laminotomy, laser laminectomy, and laser facet ablation/denervation/rhizotomy, as they are considered investigational and therefore not covered. 2. Percutaneous and endoscopic laminectomy and disc decompression procedures, including, but not limited to, percutaneous endoscopic discectomy with or without laser (PELD) (also known as arthroscopic microdiscectomy or Yeung Endoscopic Spinal Surgery System [Y.E.S.S.]) (62380), automated percutaneous lumbar discectomy (APLD) (62287), and minimally invasive percutaneous decompression (“mild®” procedure [0274T, 0275T]), as they are considered investigational and therefore not covered. 3. Devices for annulus repair or closure (i.e., disc annular repair technology [Barricaid® ACD device]) (C9757), as they are considered investigational and therefore not covered. Definitions Cauda equina syndrome – The cauda equina is a bundle of spinal nerve roots which spread out from the bottom of the spinal cord. Cauda equina syndrome is a group of symptoms that may happen if the cauda equina gets squeezed or damaged. The symptoms may include pain, numbness and weakness in the lower back and legs, foot drop, and problems controlling the bowels or bladder. Corpectomy – Surgery to remove part or the entire vertebral body and intervertebral disc material to relieve stress put on the spinal cord and spinal nerves, typically in the cervical spine. Discectomy – the partial or complete removal of an intervertebral disc. Intervertebral discs are made of rubbery tissue and are located between the vertebrae (bones) of the spinal column. Facetectomy – Surgery to remove the entire facet joint of a vertebrae in order to release pressure on spinal nerve roots. Foraminotomy – Surgery involving removal of some bone on the edge of foramen to make more space for the nerves exiting that foramen. If a portion of an intervertebral disc is seen pressing against the nerve root, a portion of the disc may be removed during this procedure. Herniated disc – is a condition in which the outer portion (annulus fibrosus) of the vertebral disc is torn, enabling the inner portion (nucleus) to herniate or extrude through the fibers. Laminectomy – Surgery to remove the lamina — the back part of the vertebra that covers the spinal canal. A type of decompression surgery, laminectomy enlarges the spinal canal to relieve pressure on the spinal cord or nerves. Laminoplasty – Surgery that increases the space within the spinal canal by creating a hinge on the lamina such that the vertebrae swing open like a door. Clinical documentation indicates presence of at least one sign/symptom, associated with the condition(s), limiting activities of daily living. The following list includes possible signs/symptoms and is not all-inclusive. A. Radiculopathy B. Neurogenic claudication C. Myelopathy D. Upper/lower extremity weakness, numbness, or pain, and 3. Conservative treatments must include physical therapy (PT), at least 4 visits over a course of 6 weeks or less, completed within the current episode of care (within the last six months, as noted above). Note: The requirement for physical therapy will not be met if there is a failure to complete prescribed physical therapy for non-clinical reasons.
